idiom_name: MutableSharedFlow with extraBufferCapacity fed by non-suspending tryEmit, false counted as a drop
implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines supplies the fan-out primitive, not the tap itself: a hot MutableSharedFlow is the recipient list - collectors are subscribers that come and go without the sender noticing (subscriptionCount observes them) - and one emitting coroutine reaches all of them. The producer side stays on the handler's own coroutine context: tryEmit never suspends, so the tap costs the primary coroutine an atomic buffer insert and nothing else; each analyzer consumes on its own dispatcher in its own coroutine (scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { taps.collect { analyze(it) } }), so analyzer latency lives entirely off the emission path, with the shared buffer as the only coupling. The copy is made by the caller before tryEmit: the API stores and shares the value it is handed, so emit m.snapshot() (defensive copy or serialized form), never the live Message. The overflow policy is a constructor choice: extraBufferCapacity = N with the default BufferOverflow.SUSPEND makes tryEmit return false exactly when a plain emit would have suspended, which is the drop event to count; BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST/DROP_LATEST also never suspend but make tryEmit return true unconditionally, silently evicting values instead - sampling by policy, invisible without a counter of your own. Default MutableSharedFlow() (no replay, no buffer) is a rendezvous bus: emit suspends until every subscriber has received, which puts analyzer latency into the primary flow - wrong for a tap. For exactly one analyzer, a Channel(capacity = N, onBufferOverflow = ...) with trySend is the leaner form: trySend never suspends or throws and the returned ChannelResult.isFailure is the counted drop, while the onUndeliveredElement callback fires for values evicted by DROP_OLDEST/DROP_LATEST, giving the counter even under a silent policy. When the service already runs on Spring Integration, its Kotlin DSL is the honest library route - integrationFlow { wireTap { handle { ... } } } installs the framework's WireTap ChannelInterceptor on the channel, sending the message to another channel without altering the flow - but the interceptor runs on the sender's thread unless the tap flow starts with an executor channel, so the coroutine form remains the local idiom outside that framework.
pitfalls: Default MutableSharedFlow() is unbuffered: emit suspends until all subscribers receive the value and tryEmit returns true only when no subscriber is attached - so a connected slow analyzer stalls the emitting coroutine, and a detached one silently discards every copy; without replay or extraBufferCapacity the tap is either coupled or lost.

tryEmit can return false only when onBufferOverflow is SUSPEND and subscribers exist: switch to DROP_OLDEST or DROP_LATEST and the same call reports success while evicting buffered values, so the overflow policy becomes invisible exactly when it starts discarding - count the false return, or count evictions via the Channel onUndeliveredElement hook.

Overflow accounting only runs when at least one subscriber lags: while no analyzer is subscribed the buffer is not used, values beyond the replay cache are dropped and tryEmit still returns true - zero counted drops does not mean zero lost copies, so expose subscriptionCount alongside the drop counter.

A shared flow hands the same object reference to every collector - nothing copies it - so emitting the live Message lets any analyzer mutate or retain what the primary path still owns; snapshot (deep-copy or serialize) at the emit site.

With the default SUSPEND strategy a plain emit suspends the producer while the bounded buffer is full, and a subscriber stuck in downstream work (not cancelled) keeps it full: the tap's backpressure then resumes the primary coroutine late - use tryEmit on the hot path and let the counted drop absorb the stall.
